cases.answer: Last winter on my orthopaedic ward we had two admissions arrive at once while I still had a full round of morning medications due and a patient waiting for discharge teaching. I was the primary nurse for six beds, so deciding the order of the work was my call. I listed every task by risk, gave the 9 o'clock insulin and pain medication first, asked the unit clerk to start the admission paperwork, and booked the discharge teaching for early afternoon with the patient's daughter present. Every medication went out inside the one-hour window and both new patients were settled by 11:30.

On a Friday afternoon in our day surgery unit, a cancelled theatre list meant four patients were recovering at once while I also owed several discharge phone calls. I was the recovery nurse responsible for those four. Everyone was home by 5 pm, no follow-up call was missed, and the usual wait fell by about 30 minutes. Next time I would ask for help at 2 pm rather than 3.

Before I sign off a care plan I go through it in the same order each time. First I read the plan against the admission assessment in the electronic health record to be sure every identified problem has a goal. Then I check that each intervention has an owner and a time, and that the allergies and fall-risk score match the chart. Finally I read the plan through with the patient or family. I do it because a missed pressure injury risk or a wrong diet order lands directly on the person in the bed.

Three years ago in our intensive care unit a woman's husband had a severe stroke, and the team agreed he would not recover. The doctor asked me to join the family meeting because I knew them best. Beforehand I reread the scan notes, asked the doctor what options we could offer, and set up a quiet room with chairs and tissues. I sat down, said plainly and early that his injury was too severe for him to survive, and then paused so she could take it in. I stayed, answered her questions and called the chaplain. The family stayed with him for two hours and she later sent the unit a card. I learned that silence after hard news is part of the message.

Say a patient refused the mobility goal in their care plan after surgery. I would first sit down and ask them to tell me what worries them, without interrupting. Then I would explain what the goal is for and the risks of skipping it in simple words, and look for a compromise, such as two shorter walks a day. The cost is that recovery may be slower than I would like, and I would accept that over forcing them, because their trust matters more. I would document the conversation and their decision in the care plan, tell the doctor, and check back next shift to see whether anything has changed.

Imagine someone who will not go along with the walking target in their post-operative care plan. To begin, I would pull up a chair and let them say what is bothering them, letting them finish. Next I would put in everyday words why the target exists and what could go wrong if they skip it, then try to meet them halfway, perhaps two brief strolls rather than one long one. What I would give up is some speed of recovery, and I would rather live with that than push them and lose their confidence. Afterwards I would put the talk and their choice in the plan, let the physician know, and look in again on the following shift.

Take a patient with diabetes who wants to keep eating sweets, against the dietary part of the care plan. I would listen to why they feel that way, perhaps it is a comfort after a hard week, and not lecture. I would explain what high glucose does and show them their last readings. We might agree one small treat after a meal on days their glucose monitoring is in range, which means I accept a looser target than ideal. I would chart the agreement, ask the dietitian to review the plan, and recheck the readings in a few days.

When a patient disagrees with the care plan, such as refusing a repositioning schedule, I let them speak fully and I never interrupt. Honestly I tell them straight away that they have to follow the plan and I cut across them when they object. I explain in plain words what repositioning prevents and put the conversation in the notes. I would ask the wound nurse to review it the next day and change the schedule if it keeps failing.

If a patient disagreed with the pain section of their care plan, for instance refusing the nerve block, no sorry, refusing the oral morphine, I would ask what they are afraid of and listen to all of it. I would explain the risk of uncontrolled pain and offer a lower dose as a middle path, accepting that their pain might not be fully controlled. I would tell the doctor, write it in the plan and review with them at the next round.

I would train a new teammate in three stages. First I would show her our care plan template in the electronic record using one of my own patients, explaining each section: problem, goal, intervention and review date. Then I would let her write a plan for a patient while I sit beside her and watch, and give feedback right afterwards. Finally she would write one alone and I would read it that evening. Good care plans matter because a vague plan means the next nurse misses a fall risk or a dressing change and the patient pays for it.

I would put assessment first when a patient might be unstable, and move education to a shorter teach-back or a later session. On a medical ward I once had a man newly started on insulin and another patient whose oxygen level was dropping. I assessed the second patient first and asked the diabetes educator to teach the insulin at 2 pm, then told the first man plainly that I would be back. I let the doctor know about the oxygen drop. It matters because missing a change in condition can cost a life, while education can usually be repeated.

If someone could be getting worse, I would look them over before anything else and shrink the teaching into a quick check-back or schedule it for later. Once, on a general medical floor, one man had just begun insulin and a different patient's oxygen reading was falling. I examined the second patient first, got the diabetes nurse specialist to cover the insulin teaching at 2 in the afternoon, and promised the first man I would return. The physician heard about the falling oxygen from me. The reason is that failing to catch a worsening condition can be fatal, whereas teaching can be done again.
